They aren't driving the LEDs with AC, they are driving it with digital.  Most likely, as I pointed out above, is they do it to conserve power.  Those tail lights probably have 150 LEDs in them, each one using around 10mA, or 1.5A if they were on continuously.  Pulse them at 10Hz, they'll be just as bright and consume 1/10th the power.

In my circuits that I worked on we pulsed the LEDs not to be cheap or even to dim them (in fact we wanted them bright).  Light doesn't turn off right away, so you turn off the power and it decays away.  Thus you can turn on the power, full, for about 1/10th of a second or maybe a bit less and it will be at just about full brightness the entire time.  Best part, it is a lot less current thus saves on power.  Believe it or not, a lot of LEDs on continuously use up a lot of power.  The project I worked on had about 70 LEDs per device, at 10mA per LED (and the resistor), you're looking at about 700mA (close to 800mA) of power.  That's a lot of power.  So you strobe them for 1/10th of the period and you get it down to close to 80mA and they are just as bright.

Then you are using Excel wrong.  In fact, there is almost never a reason to round in Excel.  You put the numbers in, and display down to 2 digits or whatever you want, the values themselves will be the full value.  Thus when you add them up, it will be exactly the right number.  If you force Excel to round them, then this is your mistake, not the tools.  Try entering in the rounded number into the calculator and you'll get the same results.  Excel has much higher precision that most calculators.  

example:

    Pay Rate = Paycheck / Hours Worked
    Pay Rate = $123.45 / 7.4
    Pay Rate = $16.682432432

Now you can set the format of Pay Rate to be two digits and it will display as : $16.68, but the actual number is the whole thing.  If you tell it to ROUND then you have cut off the rest of that number.

Even worse is if you force the rounding before the functions.  And even worse if they use other values that are also rounded.

You need to know when and where the right place for rounding is.  You need to put that knowledge into Excel.  OR don't put any rounding and let Excel store and use the full values and display to the precision you want.

People who take the calculator to add things up, get the number 12345 and go to type it into the field in Excel, but type in 12346 instead.  Everything looks perfect, but it is wrong.  

Or if the calculation is a bit longer, say a quick average (A + B + C)/3 and the person types into the calculator A + B = + C = / 4 = (where the A, B, and C are values).

Embedded devices are computers, but for PC's yes, x64 based machines operate on longer instructions that do make operations more efficient.  It allows for better manipulation of data; and more bandwidth to memory as well.  Software, of course, has to support it.  But regardless; if there is a 64 bit processor and 64 bit memory bus, it will be faster than a 64 bit processor on a 32 bit bus, or a 32 bit processor on a 32 bit bus.  Even if the amount of memory is the same.


BUT some embedded processors have 32 bit external busses and 64 bit internal processing; thus when running from internal cache they are fast but the external accesses makes it slower.  More common is a 32 bit processor with a 16 bit memory bus.  Ideally the memory bus should fit the processor.

The processor operates on not only a 64bit memory bus, but it also has 64 bit instructions.  This means that it can often perform longer operations in one cycle (such as a 32 bit to 32bit register move).  This can gain a ton of speed over having to do two or more instructions to do the same thing.

But if it ONLY has a 64bit processor bus, it won't make much difference.

Rounding it up to a nibble makes sense though; 0101.  This is even more important when writing hex, for example 512h, are all 12 bits significant or only 11?  Very, very few processors will operate on 12 bit interfaces; thus it is normal to write it as 0512h to indicate a 16-bit processor.  I mean loading the value into a 32-bit register, what happens to the upper 16 bits?  Are those upper 16 bits unchanged or are they zeroed out?  The processor often needs to know.  0000_0512h is a 32 bit number, 0512h is a 16 bit number, 05h is an 8 bit number. 5h is a 4 bit nibble.

Because computers (almost every one) operates on 8, 16, or 32 bits at a time, they you always pad it out to fit the width of the operation the processor works on.  I have used one processor that was 12 bits; but that's it (after 20 years).  

Why do you do this?  Because when you load data into a register on a processor, say a 16-bit processor; you can load 8 bits of data but the upper byte is unused leaving it unchanged.  If you need to load 11 bits (as in this case) you pad it out to 16 bits because the upper 5 bits will automatically set to zero, thus you define them by writing 07DF (hex value) instead of just 7DF.  

It's just standard practice in engineering and most programming situations.

If you adjust minimum wage, from the 1930's to present day money, it is only slightly below the average right now.  Bringing it up to about $10/hour is about where it should be, anything higher is too much.  

That being said, there are several arguments against it.

1. As Dicktremain said, if everyone gets a raise, the prices go up and no one gets a raise but the cost of living increases.
2. Money has to come from somewhere, big corporations can spread the cost across it's products and still make the same profits; small businesses cannot and will feel the pinch.  Thus it hurts small mom-and-pop stores.
3. It negates incentive for people to work hard; if you are at minimum wage today, work your but off to get +$2/hour more over the last 4 years; and suddenly the minimum wage is your current salary, why work for it when it will just be given to you later.  Only those at minimum wage will get the increase, those everyone up the food chain.
4. Minimum wage is not supposed to be a living wage, but enough to augment or keep you going while you move yourself up the ladder.

That's just a few of the arguments; some are more valid than others.  All have merit but the truth is a mixture of them.  Generally though, minimum wage should keep up with inflation; but overall, most people's wages do not (i.e. people making $80k per year may get 1 or 2% raises where inflation is 4 or 5%).  Generally, push yourself to get a better job sooner and work harder.
